tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She packed a apple in her lunchbox for the hike.
He bought an umbrella before the outdoor concert.
We need an new bicycle for the weekend trip.
The coach approved an plan for the relay team.
Please send me an email with the rehearsal times.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Apple" begins with a vowel sound, so English needs "an apple," not "a apple."

Tip: Match a/an to the sound that follows, not just the first letter on the page.

TRUE — "Umbrella" starts with a vowel sound, so "an umbrella" is the correct first-mention form.

Tip: First mention of one countable thing usually takes a/an — but only the matching form.

FALSE — "New" begins with a consonant sound (/n/), so English needs "a new bicycle," not "an new bicycle."

Tip: Adjectives do not change the a/an rule — listen to the sound right after a/an.

FALSE — "Plan" begins with a consonant sound, so use "a plan," not "an plan."

Tip: The rest of the sentence can stay; only the form before plan is wrong.

TRUE — "Email" begins with a vowel sound (/iː/), so "an email" is correct.

Tip: Say the next word aloud; if it starts with a vowel sound, use an.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is about choosing a versus an before a singular countable noun. Listen for vowel versus consonant sounds right after the determiner, including when an adjective comes first.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guide asked for an honest answer about the trail conditions.
They hired a European tutor for their French exchange.
She completed a MBA while volunteering at the library.
We reserved an hotel near the festival grounds.
He is an university student in biology.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Honest" starts with a silent h, so the spoken form begins with a vowel sound and takes "an."

Tip: Silent letters still decide a/an by sound, not spelling.

TRUE — "European" begins with a /j/ sound (like "you"), which counts as a consonant sound, so "a European" is correct.

Tip: Eu- and u- words often take a when they sound like they start with "y."

FALSE — "MBA" is normally read letter by letter, starting with /em/, a vowel sound, so it needs "an MBA."

Tip: With abbreviations, base a/an on how you pronounce the first letter.

FALSE — In standard modern pronunciation, "hotel" keeps the /h/, so "a hotel" is the usual form, not "an hotel."

Tip: Prefer a before clearly sounded h- words in contemporary English.

FALSE — "University" starts with a /j/ sound, so the correct form is "a university student."

Tip: If you can hear a "y" glide at the start, choose a.
tasks.solution_overview: These sentences turn on sound, not spelling. Silent h, letter names in abbreviations, and the "y" glide in words like European and university are the traps to watch.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I read a novel yesterday; the novel kept me awake until dawn.
Please close a window; it is freezing in here.
She joined the choir as a junior soprano in 2022.
Could you pass me a salt from the tray?
They opened an café on the corner last spring.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — First mention uses "a novel"; the second mention switches to "the novel" because the same book is now identified.

Tip: a/an introduces; the points back to something already specified.

FALSE — In this situation the window is a specific one in the room, so English expects "the window," not "a window."

Tip: When both speakers can identify the thing, prefer the.

TRUE — Roles after "as" commonly take a/an for one role among many: "as a junior soprano."

Tip: Occupations and roles usually need a/an in this pattern.

FALSE — At the table, "salt" is a specific shared item, so "the salt" is the natural choice.

Tip: Shared, obvious objects in the immediate setting take the.

FALSE — "Café" begins with a consonant sound (/k/), so use "a café," not "an café."

Tip: Spelling with a vowel letter does not override a consonant sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on whether the noun is newly introduced or already clear to both speakers. First mention and shared, obvious objects follow different patterns.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The sun was still low when the runners started.
Moon looks unusually bright tonight over the harbour.
She is only person who finished the crossword.
This is same recipe we used last winter.
He is the tallest player on the school team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Unique celestial bodies take "the": "the sun." The runners are also definite in context.

Tip: One-of-a-kind referents almost always need the.

FALSE — "Moon" in this sense needs "the moon"; leaving it bare is not standard.

Tip: Pair the with unique natural landmarks and celestial objects.

FALSE — "Only" before a singular noun requires "the only person."

Tip: Patterns with only, same, next, and last usually need the.

FALSE — The fixed pattern is "the same recipe," not bare "same recipe."

Tip: "Same" almost never stands without the in this use.

TRUE — Superlative forms take "the": "the tallest player."

Tip: If you see -est or most + adjective for a unique ranking, expect the.
tasks.solution_overview: Unique things, superlatives, and words like only and same strongly prefer the. Check whether the noun points to one identifiable item in the world or in the set.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hikers received useful advice from the ranger.
She gave me an advice about packing for cold weather.
We still need more informations before we choose a route.
The lab ordered new equipment for the science fair.
They bought an furniture for the guest room.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Advice" is uncountable, so it appears with zero article here and is modified by "useful," not by a/an.

Tip: Uncountable abstract nouns often take zero article when used in a general sense.

FALSE — "Advice" cannot take "an"; say "some advice" or "a piece of advice."

Tip: If you need a countable unit, use a piece/bit/item of + uncountable noun.

FALSE — "Information" has no plural form in standard English; use "more information," not "informations."

Tip: Watch for false plurals on uncountable nouns.

TRUE — "Equipment" is uncountable and correctly appears without a/an; "new" simply describes the mass noun.

Tip: Zero article + adjective + uncountable noun is a common correct pattern.

FALSE — "Furniture" is uncountable, so "an furniture" is impossible; use "furniture" or "a piece of furniture."

Tip: Do not place a/an directly before classic uncountables like furniture, equipment, or advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Uncountable nouns reject a/an and usually reject plural -s. Prefer zero article for general reference, or a quantifying phrase such as a piece of when you need a unit.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Progress on the mural has been slower than expected.
The news were surprising for the whole neighbourhood.
Research shows that morning light can improve mood.
We lack an evidence to support that claim.
Traffic was heavy on the way to the airport.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Progress" is uncountable and correctly used with zero article for a general process underway.

Tip: Zero article is normal with progress, research, and similar abstracts.

FALSE — "News" is uncountable and takes a singular verb: "The news was surprising." The determiner "the" can stay; the verb must agree.

Tip: "News" looks plural but behaves as singular.

TRUE — General research findings use zero article: "Research shows…"

Tip: When you mean research as a field or body of work in general, omit a/the.

FALSE — "Evidence" is uncountable, so "an evidence" is wrong; use "evidence" or "a piece of evidence."

Tip: Specificity does not make evidence countable with a/an.

TRUE — "Traffic" is uncountable and takes zero article in this general statement about conditions.

Tip: Mass nouns for weather, traffic, and similar conditions usually need no a/an.
tasks.solution_overview: Several everyday nouns are uncountable even when they end in -s or feel countable. Keep zero article for general reference and avoid a/an before evidence, progress, and traffic.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Children need clear routines at home.
The neighbours expect quieter evenings during exam week.
Water is still scarce after the long drought.
She drinks the coffee every morning before class.
Teachers should explain key ideas carefully.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Plural nouns in a general sense take zero article: "Children need…"

Tip: General plurals usually omit the.

TRUE — Here "the neighbours" can refer to the known people next door, so the is acceptable and natural.

Tip: The + plural is fine when the group is definite in context.

TRUE — Uncountable "water" used generically takes zero article.

Tip: Materials and substances in general statements often need no determiner.

FALSE — Habitual general coffee-drinking uses zero article: "She drinks coffee every morning," not "the coffee," unless a specific coffee is meant.

Tip: Do not force the onto uncountables used in a general habitual sense.

TRUE — Plural "Teachers" in a general professional statement correctly takes zero article.

Tip: Job-title plurals meaning "teachers in general" stay bare.
tasks.solution_overview: General plurals and general uncountables prefer zero article. Use the only when the group or substance is already limited to a known set.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He goes to work by bus on most weekdays.
She travelled to Lisbon by a train last Friday.
They sent the parcels by courier overnight.
I usually go to the home after the evening class.
We went to school together in the same district.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Fixed patterns "go to work" and "by bus" both use zero article.

Tip: Memorise by + transport and go to work/school/bed as zero-article chunks.

FALSE — The transport pattern is "by train," not "by a train."

Tip: After by for means of transport, do not insert a/an.

TRUE — "By courier" follows the same zero-article transport/delivery pattern.

Tip: By + service/means is typically bare.

FALSE — The fixed expression is "go home," never "go to the home" in this meaning.

Tip: Home after go/arrive/get normally takes no to and no the.

TRUE — "Go to school" with zero article means attendance as a student, which fits this sentence.

Tip: Purpose-of-institution uses often drop the.
tasks.solution_overview: Several high-frequency chunks freeze the determiner choice: by bus/train, go to work/school, and go home. Treat them as fixed patterns rather than building them word by word.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Her brother is still in hospital after the operation.
We drove past the hospital on our way to the lake.
Three activists are in the prison for peaceful protest.
The prison on the hill dates from the nineteenth century.
She stayed in bed until noon because of a migraine.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — British English uses zero article in "in hospital" when the person is there as a patient.

Tip: Purpose (patient/prisoner/student) often means zero article with the institution.

TRUE — When the building itself is meant as a location landmark, "the hospital" is correct.

Tip: Switch to the when you mean the building, not the institutional purpose.

FALSE — As inmates, the natural British pattern is "in prison," not "in the prison."

Tip: Purpose reading → zero; building reading → the.

TRUE — Referring to a specific building as a landmark correctly takes "the prison."

Tip: Physical description and location cues usually signal the building reading.

TRUE — "In bed" for resting/sleeping takes zero article in the standard idiom.

Tip: In bed / in church / in hospital follow the same purpose logic.
tasks.solution_overview: Institution nouns flip between zero article (purpose: patient, prisoner) and the (the building as a place). Read the sentence for purpose versus physical location.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She plays the piano at family gatherings.
He plays the football for the local amateur side.
They listen to the radio during the morning walk.
I watched a television until midnight after the film.
She is learning the violin with a private tutor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Musical instruments take "the" in this general ability/habit pattern: "play the piano."

Tip: play + the + instrument is the default.

FALSE — Sports use zero article: "play football," not "play the football."

Tip: Contrast instruments (the) with sports and games (zero).

TRUE — "Listen to the radio" is the standard pattern for the medium.

Tip: the radio / the news are common fixed media patterns.

FALSE — Habitual or general TV watching is "watch television," not "watch a television," unless you mean one physical set.

Tip: Medium versus device: medium often takes zero; a specific device can take a/the.

TRUE — "Learn the violin" follows the same instrument rule as play the piano.

Tip: Keep the with named instruments after play/learn.
tasks.solution_overview: Instruments prefer the; sports prefer zero. Media words like radio and television also have preferred patterns—do not invent a/an forms where the medium itself is meant.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Most students supported the later start time.
The most of guests opposed the outdoor seating plan.
Half of the cake has already been eaten.
Both finalists gave a strong closing speech.
All of luggage must be labelled before check-in.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Most" + plural noun takes zero article when speaking generally about the majority: "Most students…"

Tip: most + noun (no the) for general majorities.

FALSE — Do not say "the most of guests"; use "most of the guests" or "most guests."

Tip: After most of, you normally need the + definite noun phrase.

TRUE — "Half of the cake" correctly combines the quantifier with a definite noun phrase.

Tip: half/most/some of + the + specific noun is a safe pattern.

TRUE — "Both finalists" needs no article before both; "a strong closing speech" correctly introduces one speech each.

Tip: both/all/each have their own determiner rules—do not stack the before both.

FALSE — "All of luggage" is incomplete; write "all of the luggage" or "all luggage."

Tip: all of must be followed by a determined noun phrase (often with the).
tasks.solution_overview: Quantifier patterns interact with determiners: most + noun, most of the + noun, half of the +, and all of the +. Avoid blending those frames.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is studying economics at a well-known university.
He majored in the history before joining the museum.
They offer a course in photography this term.
The mathematics in this puzzle is unexpectedly elegant.
She teaches the English at a private college.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Academic subjects usually take zero article: "studying economics."

Tip: Subject names in general study contexts stay bare.

FALSE — As a field of study, use "history," not "the history," unless a specific history is meant.

Tip: Zero article for subjects; the only when the noun is narrowed (the history of X).

TRUE — "Photography" as a course subject correctly appears without a/the before the subject name; "a course" is the countable shell.

Tip: Count the course, not the subject noun itself.

TRUE — Here "the mathematics" refers to the specific maths in this puzzle, so the is justified.

Tip: The + subject is fine when limited by a postmodifier or clear context.

FALSE — Language subjects in general take zero article: "teaches English," not "teaches the English."

Tip: Language names as school subjects are usually bare.
tasks.solution_overview: Subject and language names are bare in general academic use, but the appears when the noun is limited to a specific body of material. Separate the countable "course" from the subject label.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The Netherlands remains a popular cycling destination.
She moved to United Kingdom after finishing her degree.
Their hostel is just outside Hague, near the sea.
We spent two weeks in Brazil last summer.
The Amazon is vital to several rainforest ecosystems.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Country names that are plural or include a common noun often take "the": "the Netherlands."

Tip: the with Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States, Philippines, etc.

FALSE — The standard form is "the United Kingdom," not bare "United Kingdom" after to.

Tip: Full political names with Kingdom/States/Republic usually need the.

FALSE — The city is "The Hague," so the sentence needs "outside The Hague."

Tip: A few place names include The as part of the name.

TRUE — Most single-name countries take zero article: "in Brazil."

Tip: Default for country and city names is zero unless the name belongs to a the-group.

TRUE — Famous rivers take "the": "the Amazon."

Tip: the with rivers, seas, oceans, and canal names.
tasks.solution_overview: Geography has compact rules: most countries and cities are bare, but plural/political names and many waterways take the. A handful of names include The as part of the proper noun.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lake Victoria appears in several geography textbooks.
They sailed across Atlantic on a freighter.
Mount Everest still attracts extreme hikers.
We spent a week in Alps after the festival.
The Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Individual lakes usually take zero article: "Lake Victoria."

Tip: Lake + name → typically zero; the Great Lakes is an exception as a group.

FALSE — Oceans and seas need "the": "the Atlantic."

Tip: the Atlantic / the Pacific / the Mediterranean.

TRUE — Mountains named with Mount take zero article: "Mount Everest."

Tip: Mount/Mt + name = zero; mountain ranges take the.

FALSE — Mountain ranges take "the": "the Alps."

Tip: Ranges and island groups usually need the.

TRUE — Deserts take "the": "the Sahara."

Tip: the Sahara / the Gobi follow the desert pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Natural features split cleanly: lakes and Mount-names are often bare; oceans, ranges, deserts, and many seas take the. Learn the groups rather than guessing per word.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Poverty remains a serious challenge in many regions.
The life is unpredictable for freelance artists.
Society must balance growth with environmental limits.
She values the honesty above everything else in friendships.
Curiosity drives long-term learning in this field.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Abstract nouns used in a general sense take zero article: "Poverty remains…"

Tip: General abstracts (poverty, society, curiosity) are usually bare.

FALSE — General "life" does not take the: "Life is unpredictable…"

Tip: Use the life only when limited (the life of an artist, the life she wanted).

TRUE — "Society" in a broad general claim correctly appears without a/the.

Tip: Zero article signals the concept as a whole.

FALSE — As a general virtue, prefer "honesty," not "the honesty," unless a specific instance is meant.

Tip: Abstract virtues in general statements stay bare.

TRUE — "Curiosity" as a general driver of learning takes zero article.

Tip: If no postmodifier narrows the abstract, omit the.
tasks.solution_overview: General abstract nouns prefer zero article. Add the only when a of-phrase or clear context turns the abstract into a specific instance.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The advice she received from her coach was unusually clear.
Equipment that arrived yesterday is still in the hallway.
An information in the appendix contradicts the summary.
The research published last week challenges our assumptions.
We need a progress before the next rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Uncountable "advice" can take "the" when a relative clause identifies a specific body of advice.

Tip: Uncountable + the is fine once the noun is made specific.

TRUE — "Equipment" remains uncountable; zero article works even with a defining relative clause when the noun is used as a mass.

Tip: You may also say "the equipment that arrived…" — both can be acceptable; bare is not wrong here.

FALSE — "Information" cannot take "an"; use "information" or "a piece of information."

Tip: Specificity does not magically make an uncountable noun countable with a/an.

TRUE — "The research published last week" correctly uses the because the postmodifier identifies a particular study set.

Tip: Postmodifiers often licence the with otherwise general uncountables.

FALSE — "Progress" is uncountable, so "a progress" is wrong; say "progress" or "some progress."

Tip: Never place a/an directly before progress.
tasks.solution_overview: Uncountables can take the when narrowed by context, but they still reject a/an. Specificity changes zero versus the, not countability itself.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was appointed the captain of the rowing club.
He became a head of the drama department after the reshuffle.
They elected her treasurer of the local book club.
She is a only photographer who stayed until closing.
He remains the unique finalist still active in round three.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — After appoint/elect/name, English often uses "the" + unique role: "appointed the captain."

Tip: Unique office titles after appoint/elect frequently take the.

FALSE — Prefer "the head of the drama department" for a unique post, or rephrase; "a head of…" sounds like one of several equal heads.

Tip: Unique organisational roles usually take the, not a.

TRUE — Zero article is also possible after elect/appoint when the title follows directly: "elected her treasurer."

Tip: Both "elected her treasurer" and "elected her the treasurer" appear; bare title after the object is standard.

FALSE — "Only" requires "the only photographer," not "a only." Also, "only" begins with a vowel sound, so a would be wrong even without that rule.

Tip: the only is a fixed determiner pattern.

FALSE — Native wording prefers "the only finalist" (or "the sole finalist"); "the unique finalist" is awkward in this ranking sense.

Tip: For exclusivity in a set, only/sole beats unique with the.
tasks.solution_overview: Titles and unique roles have special determiner habits after appoint/elect and with only. Aim for the with unique posts, and keep the only as a locked chunk.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: A number of neighbours have requested clearer recycling rules.
The number of open tickets fell after the software update.
She has a knowledge of Portuguese that helps on trips.
He has knowledge of Portuguese from years in Lisbon.
We saw a rise in visitors after the gallery redesign.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "A number of" means "several" and correctly pairs with a plural noun; the determiner pattern itself is standard.

Tip: a number of + plural is a fixed quantifying frame.

TRUE — "The number of" correctly refers to a specific total; here the noun phrase is fully determined and grammatical.

Tip: Contrast a number of (several) with the number of (the total count).

TRUE — "A knowledge of" is an accepted pattern when knowledge is limited to a field: "a knowledge of Portuguese."

Tip: Some abstracts allow a when followed by of + field.

TRUE — Zero-article "knowledge of" is equally natural for the same idea.

Tip: Both a knowledge of and knowledge of can be correct; meaning stays general-competence.

TRUE — Countable "rise" correctly takes "a" for a newly mentioned increase: "a rise in visitors."

Tip: Singular countable nouns need a determiner in this slot.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch fixed frames such as a number of versus the number of, and notice when abstracts optionally take a before of-phrases. Singular countables like rise still need a determiner.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Next week we will finalise the festival programme.
The next week we will finalise the festival programme.
In 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.
In the 1990s many families still relied on paper maps.
On Monday morning the team packs for the match.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Time expressions like "next week," "last year," and "this morning" take zero article in standard adverbial use.

Tip: next/last/this + time unit → usually zero.

FALSE — "The next week" is wrong in this future-plan adverbial; keep bare "next week."

Tip: Save the next for sequenced items inside a known series (the next slide), not for calendar next week.

FALSE — Decades need "the": "in the 1990s."

Tip: the + decade/century is the normal historical pattern.

TRUE — "In the 1990s" correctly includes the.

Tip: Same pattern for the 1800s, the twentieth century, etc.

TRUE — Days and parts of days used adverbially are often bare: "On Monday morning…"

Tip: on Monday / in summer / at night frequently take zero article.
tasks.solution_overview: Time phrases are highly patterned: next/last week stay bare, while decades and centuries take the. Do not import the into calendar adverbials where English expects zero.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She is in charge of costumes for the school play.
He was hit on head during the basketball practice.
They shook hands after settling the argument.
Please write the essay from beginning to the end carefully.
We need to keep the garden under control this summer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "In charge of costumes" uses zero article before the functional area in this common pattern.

Tip: Many be/in + noun phrases freeze without a/the (in charge, in debt, in trouble).

FALSE — Body-contact idioms take possessive or the: "on the head" / "on his head," not bare "on head."

Tip: on the + body part is the usual set phrase after verbs like hit/pat.

TRUE — "Shake hands" is a fixed zero-article idiom.

Tip: Learn hands/arms/legs idioms as chunks; do not insert the automatically.

FALSE — The paired idiom is "from beginning to end" (both bare) or "from the beginning to the end"; mixing bare beginning with "the end" is inconsistent.

Tip: Keep both sides of a fixed pair parallel in determiner choice.

TRUE — "Under control" is a zero-article prepositional idiom.

Tip: under control / in progress / on schedule are typically bare.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced accuracy often means recognising idioms where determiner choice is frozen. Prefer the set phrase over building articles logically word by word.
